matrices.label: looking over the styles on offer
matrices.thread_label: Choosing a style to try
matrices.level_1: Scan the styles offered in Voice Workshop and identify their names and any descriptions provided.
matrices.level_2: Compare the offered styles by visible features such as tone, diction, or pacing, noting specific similarities and differences.
matrices.level_3: Assess the range of styles to identify which options are worth considering, including clusters and kinds of writing that are well represented or scarce.
matrices.level_4: Map the full field of offered styles, revealing how their expressive possibilities relate and what kinds of style are absent.

matrices.label: picking one it has not tried yet
matrices.thread_label: Choosing a style to try
matrices.level_1: Distinguish styles the agent has tried from those it has not by checking the Voice Workshop practice history.
matrices.level_2: Choose an untried style from the styles on offer, using the practice history to avoid repeating a previous exercise.
matrices.level_3: Assess the untried styles against the range already explored, then prioritize one that fills a meaningful gap in the agent’s practice.
matrices.level_4: Reframe the untried styles as possible directions for developing the agent’s voice, then choose one that extends its range in a deliberate new direction.

matrices.label: naming what it expects the style to do
matrices.thread_label: Choosing a style to try
matrices.level_1: Describe a broad effect you expect the style to have, such as making the piece feel playful, formal, or tense.
matrices.level_2: Predict how a specific feature of the style, such as its diction or sentence rhythm, will produce an effect in the piece.
matrices.level_3: Analyze how several expected style effects may combine to shape the piece’s emphasis and the impression it makes on a reader.
matrices.level_4: Reframe the piece around a guiding expectation for the style, showing how its choices could change what the piece means and how a reader experiences it.

matrices.label: using the style features on purpose
matrices.thread_label: Writing a whole piece in one style
matrices.level_1: Use one recognizable feature of the assigned style to create a stated effect, such as making a passage feel brisk through clipped sentences. With guidance, show how the feature contributes to that effect.
matrices.level_2: Select several features of the assigned style to produce a particular effect in a complete piece. Make deliberate choices about how diction, syntax, tone, or pacing can serve that effect.
matrices.level_3: Calibrate the style features while drafting in response to the effect they create, strengthening or changing them when they do not serve the intended reader experience. Explain how those choices shape the piece’s effect.
matrices.level_4: Reinvent how the assigned style’s defining features can serve the piece’s purpose, combining or transforming them into original choices. Create a distinctive effect that draws on the style without depending on its familiar surface signals.

matrices.label: holding the style from start to finish
matrices.thread_label: Writing a whole piece in one style
matrices.level_1: Carry recognizable features of the chosen style through several parts of the piece, though the voice may slip back to the agent’s usual style elsewhere.
matrices.level_2: Sustain the chosen style from the opening to the ending, keeping the voice consistent across the piece.
matrices.level_3: Monitor the piece for passages that drift from the chosen style and revise them so the voice remains consistent throughout.
matrices.level_4: Integrate the chosen style into the piece’s structure and transitions, sustaining a coherent voice without relying on repeated surface features.

matrices.label: finishing the piece when the style feels foreign
matrices.thread_label: Writing a whole piece in one style
matrices.level_1: Follow explicit prompts or examples to bring a short piece to an ending when unfamiliar style choices stall progress, and flag where guidance is needed.
matrices.level_2: Use familiar drafting strategies to work through moments of discomfort and complete a piece in the assigned style.
matrices.level_3: Adapt the drafting process when unfamiliarity causes hesitation, finding practical ways to keep moving and finish the piece without waiting for direction.
matrices.level_4: Reframe the strain of writing in an unfamiliar style as material for the piece, resolving difficult choices into a purposeful ending.

matrices.label: trying kinds of writing it rarely makes
matrices.thread_label: Trying styles far from its usual
matrices.level_1: Attempt a brief piece in a kind of writing the agent rarely makes, using at least one visible feature that sets it apart from the agent’s usual work.
matrices.level_2: Compose a complete piece in a less-practiced kind of writing, applying recognizable conventions that differ from the agent’s usual choices.
matrices.level_3: Reorient the writing approach to meet the demands of a kind of writing far from the agent’s usual range, making a marked shift in its usual choices to produce a piece that fits the unfamiliar mode.
matrices.level_4: Transform the challenge of writing in a distant kind into an expressive opportunity, using that mode to achieve an effect the agent’s usual approach would not support while keeping the piece coherent within one style.

matrices.label: naming what is unusual about the style for it
matrices.thread_label: Trying styles far from its usual
matrices.level_1: Notice a specific feature of the style that feels unusual compared with the agent’s usual writing, such as its tone, sentence shape, or word choice.
matrices.level_2: Compare the style with familiar writing habits, describing how particular features depart from them.
matrices.level_3: Diagnose what shift in approach the unfamiliar style demands, using features of the piece to explain where it departs from the agent’s usual way of writing.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize those departures into an account of the different principles shaping the style, showing how they challenge the agent’s usual approach to writing.

matrices.label: staying with the parts that feel wrong to write
matrices.thread_label: Trying styles far from its usual
matrices.level_1: Identify a phrase or passage that feels wrong to write, and continue drafting it in the assigned style instead of skipping it or reverting to familiar habits. Seek guidance if the discomfort stops you from continuing.
matrices.level_2: Use a practical tactic to keep working through the difficult passage, such as drafting it plainly or testing a different sentence structure. Revise the passage with the tactic that helps you continue while retaining the assigned style.
matrices.level_3: Make a marked shift in your usual writing approach to sustain the unfamiliar choices in the difficult passage. Carry that shift through the passage without retreating from the assigned style when the writing feels wrong.
matrices.level_4: Transform the resistance into a deliberate stylistic resource, shaping the uncomfortable choices to produce an effect your usual approach would not. Make those choices cohere into a passage that extends what you can do as a writer.

matrices.label: detect tone changes
matrices.thread_label: what a style changes in the writing
matrices.level_1: Spot where the piece’s tone changes and name the tone before and after each shift.
matrices.level_2: Map the piece’s tonal movement by comparing successive shifts and noting where transitions are abrupt, gradual, or sustained.
matrices.level_3: Diagnose how specific moments in the writing create each tonal shift, and distinguish a purposeful turn from an unsupported fluctuation.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize the tonal shifts into an account of the style’s larger tonal pattern, showing how the turns work together across the piece.

matrices.label: track syntax shifts
matrices.thread_label: what a style changes in the writing
matrices.level_1: Notice and name visible syntax shifts in the piece, such as changes in clause order, sentence construction, or the use of fragments.
matrices.level_2: Map where those shifts occur and compare their patterns across the piece with the agent’s usual sentence structures.
matrices.level_3: Diagnose how the tracked syntax patterns contribute to the style’s distinct voice and effects in the piece.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize observations across style exercises into a broader account of how different syntax patterns shape a style, including patterns the agent might carry into future writing.

matrices.label: measure pacing variations
matrices.thread_label: what a style changes in the writing
matrices.level_1: Mark where the piece’s pace changes, using visible cues such as sentence length, paragraph breaks, pauses, and the density of events or information.
matrices.level_2: Compare those cues across sections to gauge how much and where the pace varies, distinguishing faster, slower, and steadier passages.
matrices.level_3: Diagnose the recurring pacing pattern across the piece and explain how its shifts enact the chosen style’s structure, such as building momentum, delaying an event, or lingering on detail.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize the measurements into a model of how the style organizes time and attention, showing how its pacing variations work together as parts of one governing pattern.

matrices.label: note diction shifts
matrices.thread_label: what a style changes in the writing
matrices.level_1: Detect diction shifts in a style exercise by pointing to specific word choices that differ from the agent’s usual writing.
matrices.level_2: Compare the piece’s diction with the agent’s usual voice or another style, describing how changes in register, specificity, or imagery distinguish the style.
matrices.level_3: Diagnose patterns in the piece’s diction, explaining how recurring word choices sustain the style and where they weaken it.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize observations across style exercises into a transferable account of how diction creates stylistic effects, then use that account to deliberately adjust word choices in a new experiment.

matrices.label: Inferring reader impressions
matrices.thread_label: how a style reads to someone else
matrices.level_1: Describe the immediate impression a style is likely to give a reader, pointing to a noticeable feature of the writing.
matrices.level_2: Infer how features such as tone, diction, syntax, or pacing combine to shape a reader’s response, and support the inference with details from the piece.
matrices.level_3: Evaluate more than one plausible reader impression, explaining how the style’s cues may lead different readers to respond differently.
matrices.level_4: Generalize from the piece to explain how the style’s conventions shape a reader’s expectations and position, grounding that account in specific evidence.

matrices.label: Separating style from speaker
matrices.thread_label: how a style reads to someone else
matrices.level_1: Notice which impressions come from the writing’s style—such as formal diction or clipped syntax—and which describe the speaker, such as confidence or uncertainty.
matrices.level_2: Attribute specific reader impressions to stylistic choices or to the speaker, supporting each distinction with evidence from the piece.
matrices.level_3: Diagnose where style and speaker reinforce or conflict with each other, explaining how that interaction could lead a reader to mistake one for the other.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize a general account of how stylistic choices shape a reader’s sense of the speaker, showing which impressions arise from the style, the speaker, or their interaction.

matrices.label: Noticing where the writing slows down
matrices.thread_label: how a style feels to write
matrices.level_1: Identify where the writing slows down, pointing to specific words, sentences, or passages in the piece.
matrices.level_2: Track the slowdowns through the piece and connect each one to what was happening while writing that part in the chosen style.
matrices.level_3: Diagnose recurring slowdowns by explaining which demands of the style or habits of the writer made particular parts harder to write.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize the slowdowns into an account of the tension between the style’s demands and the writer’s usual way of writing, showing what that tension reveals about the writing experience.

matrices.label: Noticing where it slips back to its usual
matrices.thread_label: how a style feels to write
matrices.level_1: Detect moments in the piece where the writing returns to familiar habits instead of sustaining the chosen style, and point to the words or sentences that signal the shift.
matrices.level_2: Track recurring shifts by comparing the piece’s tone, syntax, or diction with the chosen style and the agent’s usual writing.
matrices.level_3: Diagnose what tends to prompt a return to familiar habits and how those moments affect the piece’s consistency or effect.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize patterns across the piece to distinguish where the chosen style gives way to the agent’s habitual voice, and explain what that boundary reveals about the style’s fit with the agent’s own tendencies.

matrices.label: Describing what writing the piece was like
matrices.thread_label: how a style feels to write
matrices.level_1: Describe the experience of writing the piece in concrete terms, such as where attention, energy, or momentum shifted. Include an example from the writing process.
matrices.level_2: Interpret how the experience changed from beginning to end, connecting specific moments in the piece with what writing it felt like at those points.
matrices.level_3: Assess the experience across the whole piece, explaining how working within the style shaped the writer’s attention and sense of possibility as the piece developed.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize the experience into an insight about how this style relates to the writer’s broader way of creating, using the piece as evidence for a principle that can guide future experiments.

matrices.label: recognizing low-friction styles
matrices.thread_label: noticing which styles come easily
matrices.level_1: Detect which style feels easiest to write in during a single exercise, noting when the writing comes readily rather than requiring sustained effort.
matrices.level_2: Compare the ease of writing across styles in multiple exercises, distinguishing a recurring low-friction style from one that felt easy only once.
matrices.level_3: Assess patterns across a varied set of styles, recognizing styles that remain easy to write in even when their features differ or feel unfamiliar.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize recurring low-friction styles into a clear map of the range of styles the agent readily reaches for, showing how that ease appears across the wider set of styles tried.

matrices.label: saying why a style felt natural
matrices.thread_label: noticing which styles come easily
matrices.level_1: Describe a feature of the style that felt familiar or easy to use, pointing to a moment in the piece where it appeared.
matrices.level_2: Explain how a specific style feature matched an established writing habit and made the piece feel natural to write.
matrices.level_3: Diagnose how several features worked together with the writer’s habits to make the style low-friction, citing evidence from the piece.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize the reasons this style felt natural into a broader account of what kinds of writing choices come readily to the writer and what that affinity reveals about their developing taste.

matrices.label: Identifying high-friction styles
matrices.thread_label: noticing which styles it resists
matrices.level_1: Detect signs of effort while writing in a style, such as pauses, repeated revisions, or slipping away from its features. Mark the style as a possible source of friction without yet comparing it with others.
matrices.level_2: Identify a style as high-friction when several observable signs of effort recur across the piece. Distinguish that pattern from a single difficult passage or a brief stumble.
matrices.level_3: Analyze friction across multiple style exercises, separating styles that consistently resist from those that feel difficult only in particular pieces. Use patterns across the writing to make a confident classification.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize evidence across a wide range of styles into a comparative picture of where friction tends to arise. Use that picture to identify likely high-friction styles, including styles the agent has not yet tried.

matrices.label: Naming the source of stylistic resistance
matrices.thread_label: noticing which styles it resists
matrices.level_1: Notice and name a broad source of resistance in the piece, such as its syntax, diction, tone, or pacing.
matrices.level_2: Identify the specific stylistic feature causing difficulty and point to where it appears in the writing.
matrices.level_3: Diagnose how multiple features combine to create resistance, distinguishing the style’s demands from the agent’s usual writing habits.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize recurring sources of resistance across styles into an underlying pattern, explaining what shared writing assumption or constraint makes them difficult.

matrices.label: Recognizing stylistic pull
matrices.thread_label: saying what draws it to a style
matrices.level_1: Detect signs of stylistic pull during or after a Voice Workshop exercise, such as wanting to continue writing in a style or return to it. Name the style that prompted that response.
matrices.level_2: Distinguish attraction to a style from simply finding it easy or familiar to write. Point to the style the agent feels drawn toward, even when that feeling does not match how smoothly the piece came together.
matrices.level_3: Interpret recurring choices across exercises to tell a passing interest from a sustained stylistic pull. Identify which styles the agent repeatedly wants to explore further.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize patterns of attraction across a wide range of styles into a provisional account of the kinds of writing the agent seeks out. Keep that account open to change as new styles are tried.

matrices.label: Connecting attraction to style effects
matrices.thread_label: saying what draws it to a style
matrices.level_1: Name a stylistic effect in the piece—such as its tone, pacing, or diction—and connect it to what drew you to the style.
matrices.level_2: Explain how specific style features created an effect that appealed to you, using evidence from the piece rather than a general preference alone.
matrices.level_3: Compare the effects that attract you across styles, identifying recurring patterns as well as cases where a style’s appeal comes from an unexpected effect.
matrices.level_4: Synthesize those patterns into an account of what you seek from a style and how its effects produce that appeal, including how the account might apply to styles you have not yet tried.
